claim: STING plays an important role in innate immunity by controlling type I interferon response against invaded pathogens.
source: Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) plays an important role in innate immunity by controlling type I interferon response against invaded pathogens.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction (Ishikawa and Barber, 2008; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2009; Tanaka and Chen, 2012; Zhong et al., 2008).

claim: Flies with STING deletion are sensitive to starvation.
source: Flies with STING deletion are sensitive to starvation and oxidative stress, have reduced lipid storage, and downregulated expression of lipid metabolism genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Flies with STING deletion are sensitive to oxidative stress.
source: Flies with STING deletion are sensitive to starvation and oxidative stress, have reduced lipid storage, and downregulated expression of lipid metabolism genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Flies with STING deletion have reduced lipid storage.
source: Flies with STING deletion are sensitive to starvation and oxidative stress, have reduced lipid storage, and downregulated expression of lipid metabolism genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A (TAG levels) and Figure 2E,E' (lipid droplet staining).

claim: Flies with STING deletion have downregulated expression of lipid metabolism genes.
source: Flies with STING deletion are sensitive to starvation and oxidative stress, have reduced lipid storage, and downregulated expression of lipid metabolism genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray analysis data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Drosophila STING interacts with acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC).
source: We found that Drosophila STING interacts with lipid synthesizing enzymes acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FASN).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4A and mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Drosophila STING interacts with fatty acid synthase (FASN).
source: We found that Drosophila STING interacts with lipid synthesizing enzymes acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FASN).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4B and mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: ACC and FASN interact with each other.
source: ACC and FASN also interact with each other, indicating that all three proteins may be components of a large multi-enzyme complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The deletion of Drosophila STING leads to disturbed ACC localization.
source: The deletion of Drosophila STING leads to disturbed ACC localization and decreased FASN enzyme activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A,B,C.

claim: The deletion of Drosophila STING leads to decreased FASN enzyme activity.
source: The deletion of Drosophila STING leads to disturbed ACC localization and decreased FASN enzyme activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: dSTINGΔ allele contains deletion of 589 base pairs including start codon, first exon, and part of the second exon.
source: dSTINGΔ allele contained deletion of 589 base pairs including start codon, first exon, and part of the second exon (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Homozygous dSTINGΔ mutant flies are viable with no obvious observable phenotype.
source: Homozygous dSTINGΔ mutant flies are viable with no obvious observable phenotype.
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the Results section.

claim: The expression of GFP-dSTING partially or entirely rescued the sensitivity of dSTINGΔ deletion flies to both starvation and oxidative stress.
source: Importantly, the expression of GFP-dSTING partially or entirely rescued the sensitivity of dSTINGΔ deletion flies to both starvation and oxidative stress (Figure 1B,C), suggesting that the observed phenotypes are caused by dSTING deficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The deletion of dSTING had no effect on the total lifespan of fed flies in both males and females.
source: The deletion of dSTING had no effect on the total lifespan of fed flies in both males and females.
evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The age-related mortality was slightly reduced in dSTINGΔ flies, especially for the females.
source: Moreover, the age-related mortality was slightly reduced, especially for the females (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of lifespan curves in Figure 1D.

claim: Under axenic condition dSTINGΔ mutants exhibited the same response to the starvation and oxidative stress as dSTINGΔ non-axenic flies.
source: We found that under axenic condition dSTINGΔ mutants exhibited the same response to the starvation and oxidative stress as dSTINGΔ non-axenic flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Diminished immune response against bacteria is not likely to be the cause of the observed starvation and oxidative stress phenotypes.
source: This suggests that diminished immune response against bacteria is not likely to be the cause of the observed phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the axenic fly experiments showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Under fed conditions, TAG level was decreased twofold in dSTINGΔ mutants compared with the control flies.
source: Under fed conditions, TAG level was decreased twofold in dSTINGΔ mutants compared with the control flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by TAG measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Under starved conditions, TAG level dropped dramatically to about 1/8 of the level in the control flies.
source: Under starved conditions, TAG level dropped dramatically to about 1/8 of the level in the control flies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TAG measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Glycogen levels were significantly decreased in dSTINGΔ mutants in both fed and starved flies.
source: Glycogen and trehalose levels were also significantly decreased in dSTINGΔ mutants in both fed and starved flies (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by glycogen measurement data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Trehalose levels were significantly decreased in dSTINGΔ mutants in both fed and starved flies.
source: Glycogen and trehalose levels were also significantly decreased in dSTINGΔ mutants in both fed and starved flies (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by trehalose measurement data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Glucose level was increased in dSTINGΔ mutants under fed condition.
source: Interestingly, glucose level was increased under fed condition (Figure 2D, fed), suggesting that dSTINGΔ mutant flies might have either a decreased incorporation of ingested glucose into trehalose or glycogen, or an increased breakdown of these storage molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: When flies were starved for 24 hr, glucose level in dSTINGΔ mutants dropped and was twofold lower than in control flies.
source: Nevertheless, when flies were starved for 24 hr, glucose level in dSTINGΔ mutants dropped and was twofold lower than in control flies (Figure 2D, starved).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the fed flies, the expression of GFP-tagged dSTING partially rescued the mutant phenotypes for all measured metabolites.
source: In the fed flies, the expression of GFP-tagged dSTING partially rescued the mutant phenotypes for all measured metabolites (Figure 2A–D, fed).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurement data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Under starved condition, the rescue was observed only for TAG level.
source: However, under starved condition, the rescue was observed only for TAG level (Figure 2A–D, starved).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurement data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Axenic dSTINGΔ mutants showed decreased TAG and glycogen levels as compared to the axenic control flies.
source: Importantly, axenic dSTINGΔ mutants still showed decreased TAG and glycogen levels as compared to the axenic control flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), suggesting that the lowered storage metabolite levels are not due to the diminished immune response against bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: The lowered storage metabolite levels are not due to the diminished immune response against bacteria.
source: Importantly, axenic dSTINGΔ mutants still showed decreased TAG and glycogen levels as compared to the axenic control flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), suggesting that the lowered storage metabolite levels are not due to the diminished immune response against bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the axenic fly experiments showing decreased metabolite levels.

claim: Fat bodies of dSTINGΔ mutant flies contained significantly fewer lipids as compared to the control flies.
source: Fat bodies of dSTINGΔ mutant flies contained significantly fewer lipids as compared to the control flies (Figure 2E,E').
evidence: This claim is supported by Nile Red staining data shown in Figure 2E,E'.

claim: Lipid droplet content in midguts was not decreased in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: Interestingly, lipid droplet content in midguts was not decreased in dSTINGΔ mutants (Figure 2F,F'), indicating that only the fat body lipid storage was affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by Nile Red staining data shown in Figure 2F,F'.

claim: Only the fat body lipid storage was affected in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: Interestingly, lipid droplet content in midguts was not decreased in dSTINGΔ mutants (Figure 2F,F'), indicating that only the fat body lipid storage was affected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that midgut lipid content was not decreased.

claim: Flies with reduced dSTING expression specifically in fat body were more susceptible to the starvation stress and oxidative stress.
source: Flies with reduced dSTING expression specifically in fat body were more susceptible to the starvation stress and oxidative stress, and had reduced TAG and glycogen levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), highlighting the role of dSTING in fat body functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Flies with reduced dSTING expression specifically in fat body had reduced TAG and glycogen levels.
source: Flies with reduced dSTING expression specifically in fat body were more susceptible to the starvation stress and oxidative stress, and had reduced TAG and glycogen levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), highlighting the role of dSTING in fat body functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Under fed conditions, microarray analysis revealed a significant change in 672 transcripts (more than 1.4 fold change), with 381 transcripts expressed at reduced levels and 291 transcripts at elevated levels.
source: Under fed conditions, microarray analysis revealed a significant change in 672 transcripts (more than 1.4 fold change), with 381 transcripts expressed at reduced levels and 291 transcripts at elevated levels.
evidence: This claim is based on microarray analysis data.

claim: Under starved conditions, the expression of 1452 genes was altered in dSTINGΔ mutants, with 797 downregulated and 655 upregulated genes.
source: Under starved conditions, the expression of 1452 genes was altered in dSTINGΔ mutants, with 797 downregulated and 655 upregulated genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is based on microarray analysis data.

claim: The dSTING knockout and the starvation induced similar changes in gene expression.
source: Interestingly, the dSTINGΔ fed and the control starved groups clustered together along PC1 axis, indicating that the dSTING knockout and the starvation induced similar changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: dSTINGΔ mutants are characterized by the downregulation of immune response genes, including AMPs.
source: In agreement with the previous report, dSTINGΔ mutants are characterized by the downregulation of immune response genes, including AMPs (Mtk, Drs, AttD, DptB, BomS1), peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs, such as PGRP-SD and PGRP-SA), and serpins (Spn53F, Spn42De) (Supplementary file 1; Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by microarray data and previous citation (Martin et al., 2018).

claim: Based on the Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, metabolic processes and immune response genes were downregulated in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: Based on the Gene Ontology (GO) analysis, metabolic processes and immune response genes were downregulated in dSTINGΔ mutants (Figure 3B, downregulated gene sets).
evidence: This claim is based on GO analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upregulated genes were enriched with GO classifications related to cell signaling (e.g. transport, cell communication and synapse organization).
source: Upregulated genes were enriched with GO classifications related to cell signaling (e.g. transport, cell communication and synapse organization) (Figure 3B, upregulated gene sets).
evidence: This claim is based on GO analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The metabolism of lipids, particularly fatty acids, was among top scoring gene sets downregulated in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: We analyzed dSTINGΔ mutants versus control flies under fed conditions using GSEA approach and found that the metabolism of lipids, particularly fatty acids, was among top scoring gene sets downregulated in dSTINGΔ mutants (Figure 3C, downregulated gene sets).
evidence: This claim is based on GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Several proteins with a high score were identified from immunoprecipitation, including FASN 1 and 2 (CG3523 and CG3524, respectively), ACC (CG11198), and dSTING itself (CG1667).
source: Several proteins with a high score were identified, including FASN 1 and 2 (CG3523 and CG3524, respectively), ACC (CG11198), and dSTING itself (CG1667) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is based on mass spectrometry analysis data.

claim: ACC catalyzes the formation of malonyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA, the first committed step of fatty acid synthesis.
source: ACC catalyzes the formation of malonyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA, the first committed step of fatty acid synthesis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge cited in the manuscript (López-Lara and Soto, 2019; Wakil and Abu-Elheiga, 2009).

claim: FASN uses malonyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA to synthesize palmitic fatty acid.
source: The next step is performed by FASN, which uses malonyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA to synthesize palmitic fatty acid.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Both ACC and FASN co-immunoprecipitated with GFP-dSTING.
source: We confirmed the mass spec results by performing the immunoprecipitation from the abdomens of adult flies expressing GFP-dSTING in fat body. Both ACC and FASN co-immunoprecipitated with GFP-dSTING (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: ACC and FASN interacted with each other in control flies.
source: Interestingly, we found that ACC and FASN interacted with each other as showed by the reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4C,D). We observed this interaction not only in control flies but also in dSTINGΔ mutants flies with or without the expression of GFP-dSTING.
evidence: This claim is supported by reciprocal immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: ACC and FASN interacted with each other in dSTINGΔ mutants flies with or without the expression of GFP-dSTING.
source: Interestingly, we found that ACC and FASN interacted with each other as showed by the reciprocal immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4C,D). We observed this interaction not only in control flies but also in dSTINGΔ mutants flies with or without the expression of GFP-dSTING.
evidence: This claim is supported by reciprocal immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: ACC protein level and activity were not significantly changed in dSTINGΔ mutants flies.
source: We measured ACC and FASN activity in adult flies. ACC protein level and activity were not significantly changed in dSTINGΔ mutants flies (Figure 5A,A').
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay and western blot data shown in Figure 5A,A'.

claim: FASN activity was almost two times lower in dSTINGΔ mutants as compared to the control flies.
source: However, FASN activity was almost two times lower in dSTINGΔ mutants as compared to the control flies (Figure 5B), but the protein level was unchanged (Figure 5B').
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: FASN protein level was unchanged in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: However, FASN activity was almost two times lower in dSTINGΔ mutants as compared to the control flies (Figure 5B), but the protein level was unchanged (Figure 5B').
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B'.

claim: The expression of GFP-tagged dSTING on dSTINGΔ mutant background restored FASN activity to the control level.
source: Importantly, the expression of GFP-tagged dSTING on dSTINGΔ mutant background restored FASN activity to the control level (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Malonyl-CoA level was significantly increased in dSTINGΔ flies.
source: Polar metabolite profiling of dSTINGΔ flies compared to control flies showed that indeed, malonyl-CoA level was significantly increased, whereas acetyl-CoA level remained unchanged in the mutants (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by polar metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acetyl-CoA level remained unchanged in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: Polar metabolite profiling of dSTINGΔ flies compared to control flies showed that indeed, malonyl-CoA level was significantly increased, whereas acetyl-CoA level remained unchanged in the mutants (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by polar metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP tagged dSTING co-sedimented exclusively with the membrane fraction.
source: To check whether this is also the case in Drosophila, we performed membrane fractionation, which showed that GFP tagged dSTING co-sedimented exclusively with the membrane fraction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane fractionation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP-dSTING mostly co-localized with the ER and to the lesser extent with the Golgi, but not with the cellular membrane in Drosophila S2 tissue culture cells.
source: We also expressed GFP-dSTING in Drosophila S2 tissue culture cells and found that it mostly co-localized with the ER and to the lesser extent with the Golgi, but not with the cellular membrane (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), in agreement with previous observation (Goto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and previous citation (Goto et al., 2018).

claim: GFP-dSTING mainly co-localized with Calnexin at the cortex in fat body cells.
source: GFP-dSTING mainly co-localized with Calnexin at the cortex. Little or no signal was observed at the perinuclear region of fat body cells (Figure 6A,A').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A,A'.

claim: Both ACC and FASN partially co-localized with GFP-dSTING at the cell periphery region of the ER.
source: Both ACC and FASN partially co-localized with GFP-dSTING at the cell periphery region of the ER (Figure 6B, B', C and C').
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B,B',C,C'.

claim: In dSTINGΔ mutant cells ACC concentrated in the perinuclear region with a minimal signal in the cell periphery.
source: While ACC extended throughout wild-type cells, in dSTINGΔ mutant cells ACC concentrated in the perinuclear region with a minimal signal in the cell periphery (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The expression of GFP-dSTING on dSTING null background normalized ACC staining toward the wild-type distribution.
source: The expression of GFP-dSTING on dSTING null background normalized ACC staining toward the wild-type distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In dSTINGΔ mutants, ACC appeared disorganized and aggregated compared with the wild-type cells and cells expressing GFP-dSTING.
source: A closer examination of the perinuclear region of the fat body cells revealed that in dSTINGΔ mutants, ACC appeared disorganized and aggregated compared with the wild-type cells and cells expressing GFP-dSTING (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: 67% of nuclei had a perinuclear 'aggregated' ACC phenotype in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: The quantifications showed that 67% of nuclei had a perinuclear 'aggregated' ACC phenotype (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: FASN maintained its localization pattern in dSTINGΔ mutant cells.
source: On the other hand, FASN maintained its localization pattern in dSTINGΔ mutant cells (Figure 7D), but partially co-localized with ACC 'aggregates' (Figure 7E), in agreement with the immunoprecipitation results (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: FASN partially co-localized with ACC 'aggregates' in dSTINGΔ mutant cells.
source: On the other hand, FASN maintained its localization pattern in dSTINGΔ mutant cells (Figure 7D), but partially co-localized with ACC 'aggregates' (Figure 7E), in agreement with the immunoprecipitation results (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The core components of STING pathway evolved more than 600 million years ago, before the evolution of type I IFNs.
source: However, recent studies showed that the core components of STING pathway evolved more than 600 million years ago, before the evolution of type I IFNs (Wu et al., 2014; Margolis et al., 2017; Morehouse et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Wu et al., 2014; Margolis et al., 2017; Morehouse et al., 2020).

claim: Enzymes that are involved in sequential reactions often physically interact with each other and form larger multi-enzyme complexes.
source: Enzymes that are involved in sequential reactions often physically interact with each other and form larger multi-enzyme complexes, which facilitates the substrate channeling and efficient regulation of the pathway flux (Schmitt and An, 2017; Kastritis and Gavin, 2018; Sweetlove and Fernie, 2018; Zhang and Fernie, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Schmitt and An, 2017; Kastritis and Gavin, 2018; Sweetlove and Fernie, 2018; Zhang and Fernie, 2021).

claim: ACC, ACL (ATP citrate lyase), and FASN physically associated in the microsomal fraction of rat liver.
source: ACC, ACL (ATP citrate lyase), and FASN physically associated in the microsomal fraction of rat liver (Gillevet and Dakshinamurti, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Gillevet and Dakshinamurti, 1982).

claim: A lipogenic protein complex including ACC, FASN, and four more enzymes was isolated from the oleaginous fungus Cunninghamella bainieri.
source: Moreover, in the recent work, a lipogenic protein complex including ACC, FASN, and four more enzymes was isolated from the oleaginous fungus Cunninghamella bainieri (Shuib et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Shuib et al., 2018).

claim: MIG12 overexpression in livers of mice increased total fatty acid synthesis and hepatic triglyceride content.
source: MIG12 overexpression in livers of mice increased total fatty acid synthesis and hepatic triglyceride content (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Kim et al., 2010).

claim: MIG12 protein binds to ACC and facilitates its polymerization thus enhancing the activity of ACC.
source: It has been shown that MIG12 protein binds to ACC and facilitates its polymerization thus enhancing the activity of ACC (Kim et al., 2010; Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Kim et al., 2010; Park et al., 2013).

claim: All four proteins – ACC, FASN, MIG12, and Spot14 – exist as a part of a multimeric complex.
source: Importantly, there is an evidence that all four proteins – ACC, FASN, MIG12, and Spot14 – exist as a part of a multimeric complex (McKean, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (McKean, 2016).

claim: Drosophila STING might 'anchor' ACC and FASN possibly together with other enzymes at the ER membrane.
source: We propose that dSTING might 'anchor' ACC and FASN possibly together with other enzymes at the ER membrane.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the interaction and localization data.

claim: The resulting complex facilitates fatty acid synthesis by allowing for a quicker transfer of malonyl-CoA product of ACC to the active site of FASN.
source: The resulting complex facilitates fatty acid synthesis by allowing for a quicker transfer of malonyl-CoA product of ACC to the active site of FASN.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: In dSTINGΔ mutants, ACC loses its association with some regions of the ER resulting in the weakened interaction between ACC and FASN.
source: In dSTINGΔ mutants, ACC loses its association with some regions of the ER resulting in the weakened interaction between ACC and FASN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and interaction data.

claim: Less FASN immunoprecipitated with ACC in dSTINGΔ mutants compared to control flies.
source: We did observe less FASN immunoprecipitated with ACC in dSTINGΔ mutants compared to control flies, and the opposite effect was found in flies expressing GFP-tagged dSTING (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The opposite effect was found in flies expressing GFP-tagged dSTING (more FASN immunoprecipitated with ACC).
source: We did observe less FASN immunoprecipitated with ACC in dSTINGΔ mutants compared to control flies, and the opposite effect was found in flies expressing GFP-tagged dSTING (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: De novo synthesis of fatty acids continuously contributes to the total fat body TAG storage in Drosophila.
source: It has been shown that de novo synthesis of fatty acids continuously contributes to the total fat body TAG storage in Drosophila (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Wicker-Thomas et al., 2015; Parvy et al., 2012; Garrido et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Wicker-Thomas et al., 2015; Parvy et al., 2012; Garrido et al., 2015).

claim: The reduced fatty acid synthesis due to the lowered FASN enzyme activity in dSTINGΔ deletion mutants might be responsible for the decreased TAG lipid storage and starvation sensitivity phenotypes.
source: We hypothesize that the reduced fatty acid synthesis due to the lowered FASN enzyme activity in dSTINGΔ deletion mutants might be responsible for the decreased TAG lipid storage and starvation sensitivity phenotypes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed phenotypes.

claim: Lipid droplets (consisting mainly of TAGs) provide protection against reactive oxygen species.
source: Evidences exist that the lipid droplets (consisting mainly of TAGs) provide protection against reactive oxygen species (Bailey et al., 2015; Jarc et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bailey et al., 2015; Jarc et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2015b).

claim: Flies with ACC RNAi are sensitive to the oxidative stress.
source: Furthermore, flies with ACC RNAi are found to be sensitive to the oxidative stress (Katewa et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Katewa et al., 2012).

claim: Both ACC and FASN are known to be regulated by phosphorylation/dephosphorylation.
source: Both proteins are known to be regulated by phosphorylation/dephosphorylation (Horton et al., 2002; Brownsey et al., 2006; Tong, 2005; Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Horton et al., 2002; Brownsey et al., 2006; Tong, 2005; Jin et al., 2010).

claim: In mammals, STING is an adaptor protein that transmits an upstream signal by interacting with kinase TBK1.
source: In mammals, STING is an adaptor protein that transmits an upstream signal by interacting with kinase TBK1 (TANK-binding kinase 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian STING.

claim: When in a complex with STING, TBK1 activates and phosphorylates IRF3 allowing its nuclear translocation and transcriptional response.
source: When in a complex with STING, TBK1 activates and phosphorylates IRF3 allowing its nuclear translocation and transcriptional response (Tanaka and Chen, 2012; Liu et al., 2015a; Zhong et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Tanaka and Chen, 2012; Liu et al., 2015a; Zhong et al., 2008).

claim: In Drosophila, STING might recruit a yet unidentified kinase that phosphorylates ACC and/or FASN thereby changing their enzymatic activity.
source: It is possible that in Drosophila, STING recruits a yet unidentified kinase that phosphorylates ACC and/or FASN thereby changing their enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: STING palmitoylation was identified as a posttranslational modification necessary for STING signaling in mice.
source: STING palmitoylation was recently identified as a posttranslational modification necessary for STING signaling in mice (Mukai et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Mukai et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2018).

claim: Palmitic acid synthesized by FASN might participate in the regulation of dSTING possibly providing a feedback loop.
source: In this way, palmitic acid synthesized by FASN might participate in the regulation of dSTING possibly providing a feedback loop.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on the palmitoylation of STING.

claim: Malonyl-CoA is a key regulator of the energy metabolism.
source: The product of ACC – malonyl-CoA – is a key regulator of the energy metabolism (Saggerson, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Saggerson, 2008).

claim: During lipogenic conditions, ACC is active and produces malonyl-CoA, which provides the carbon source for the synthesis of fatty acids by FASN.
source: During lipogenic conditions, ACC is active and produces malonyl-CoA, which provides the carbon source for the synthesis of fatty acids by FASN.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: In dSTING knockout, FASN activity is decreased and malonyl-CoA is not utilized and builds up in the cells.
source: In dSTING knockout, FASN activity is decreased and malonyl-CoA is not utilized and builds up in the cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enzyme activity and metabolite data.

claim: Malonyl-CoA is a potent inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase CPT1.
source: Malonyl-CoA is also a potent inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase CPT1, the enzyme that controls the rate of fatty acid entry into the mitochondria, and hence is a key determinant of the rate of fatty acid oxidation (McGarry and Brown, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (McGarry and Brown, 1997).

claim: A high level of malonyl-CoA results in a decreased fatty acid utilization for the energy.
source: Thus, a high level of malonyl-CoA results in a decreased fatty acid utilization for the energy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known inhibitory effect of malonyl-CoA on CPT1.

claim: The down-regulation of lipid catabolism genes observed in dSTINGΔ mutants might be explained by high level of malonyl-CoA.
source: This might explain the down-regulation of lipid catabolism genes that we observed in dSTINGΔ mutants (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the high malonyl-CoA level to the gene expression changes.

claim: A reduced fatty acid oxidation shifts cells to the increased reliance on glucose as a source of energy.
source: A reduced fatty acid oxidation in turn shifts cells to the increased reliance on glucose as a source of energy.
evidence: This is an inference based on metabolic principles.

claim: An increased glucose level was observed in fed dSTINGΔ mutant flies.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observed an increased glucose level in fed dSTINGΔ mutant flies (Figure 2D), as well as increased levels of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurement data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increased levels of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) were observed in dSTINGΔ mutant flies.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observed an increased glucose level in fed dSTINGΔ mutant flies (Figure 2D), as well as increased levels of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolite measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PEP level was shown to correlate with the level of glucose.
source: PEP is produced during glycolysis, and its level was shown to correlate with the level of glucose (Moreno-Felici et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Moreno-Felici et al., 2019).

claim: A reliance on glucose for the energy has a consequence of reduced incorporation of glucose into trehalose and glycogen for storage.
source: A reliance on glucose for the energy also has a consequence of reduced incorporation of glucose into trehalose and glycogen for storage, and therefore, lower levels of these storage metabolites, which we observed (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the increased glucose utilization to the decreased storage metabolites.

claim: The expression level and activity of STING were upregulated in livers of mice with high-fat diet-induced obesity.
source: The expression level and activity of STING were upregulated in livers of mice with high-fat diet-induced obesity (Bai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Bai et al., 2017).

claim: STING expression was increased in livers from nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) patients compared to control group.
source: STING expression was increased in livers from nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) patients compared to control group (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Luo et al., 2018).

claim: In nonalcoholic steatohepatitis mouse livers, STING mRNA level was elevated.
source: In nonalcoholic steatohepatitis mouse livers, STING mRNA level was also elevated (Xiong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Xiong et al., 2019).

claim: STING deficiency ameliorated metabolic phenotypes and decreased lipid accumulation, inflammation, and apoptosis in fatty liver hepatocytes.
source: Importantly, STING deficiency ameliorated metabolic phenotypes and decreased lipid accumulation, inflammation, and apoptosis in fatty liver hepatocytes (Iracheta-Vellve et al., 2016; Petrasek et al., 2013; Qiao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Iracheta-Vellve et al., 2016; Petrasek et al., 2013; Qiao et al., 2018).

claim: The prevailing hypothesis is that the obesity leads to a mitochondrial stress and a subsequent mtDNA release into the cytoplasm, which activates cGAS-STING pathway.
source: The prevailing hypothesis is that the obesity leads to a mitochondrial stress and a subsequent mtDNA release into the cytoplasm, which activates cGAS-STING pathway (Bai et al., 2017; Bai and Liu, 2019; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bai et al., 2017; Bai and Liu, 2019; Yu et al., 2019).

claim: The resulting chronic sterile inflammation is responsible for the development of NAFLD, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes.
source: The resulting chronic sterile inflammation is responsible for the development of NAFLD, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes.
evidence: This is part of the prevailing hypothesis about STING's role in obesity-related metabolic diseases.

claim: In this case, the effect of STING on metabolism is indirect and mediated by inflammation effectors.
source: In this case, the effect of STING on metabolism is indirect and mediated by inflammation effectors.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism in the prevailing hypothesis.

claim: The data presented in the current study strongly suggest that in Drosophila, STING protein is directly involved in lipid metabolism by interacting with the enzymes involved in a lipid biosynthesis.
source: The data presented in the current study strongly suggest that in Drosophila, STING protein is directly involved in lipid metabolism by interacting with the enzymes involved in a lipid biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: STING is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated transmembrane protein.
source: STimulator of INterferon Genes (STING) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated transmembrane protein that plays an important role in innate immune response by controlling the transcription of many host defense genes (Ishikawa and Barber, 2008; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2009; Tanaka and Chen, 2012; Zhong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CDNs bind to STING activating it.
source: CDNs bind to STING activating it (Wu et al., 2013; Burdette et al., 2011), and the following signaling cascade results in NF-κB- and IRF3-dependent expression of immune response molecules such as type I interferons (IFNs) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (Sun et al., 2009; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Wu et al., 2013; Burdette et al., 2011).

claim: The following signaling cascade results in NF-κB- and IRF3-dependent expression of immune response molecules such as type I interferons (IFNs) and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: CDNs bind to STING activating it (Wu et al., 2013; Burdette et al., 2011), and the following signaling cascade results in NF-κB- and IRF3-dependent expression of immune response molecules such as type I interferons (IFNs) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (Sun et al., 2009; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Sun et al., 2009; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2015a).

claim: Bacteria that invade the cell produce CDNs that directly activate STING pathway.
source: Bacteria that invade the cell are also known to produce CDNs that directly activate STING pathway (Sauer et al., 2011; Woodward et al., 2010; Danilchanka and Mekalanos, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Sauer et al., 2011; Woodward et al., 2010; Danilchanka and Mekalanos, 2013).

claim: DNA that has leaked from the damaged nuclei or mitochondria can activate STING signaling and inflammatory response.
source: Additionally, DNA that has leaked from the damaged nuclei or mitochondria can also activate STING signaling and inflammatory response, which, if excessive or unchecked, might lead to the development of autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis (Ahn et al., 2012; Kawane et al., 2006; Jeremiah et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Ahn et al., 2012; Kawane et al., 2006; Jeremiah et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: STING homologs are present in almost all animal phyla.
source: STING homologs are present in almost all animal phyla (Wu et al., 2014; Margolis et al., 2017; Kranzusch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Wu et al., 2014; Margolis et al., 2017; Kranzusch et al., 2015).

claim: The role of STING in the innate immunity of insects has been just recently identified.
source: This protein has been extensively studied in mammalian immune response; however, the role of STING in the innate immunity of insects has been just recently identified (Hua et al., 2018; Goto et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Hua et al., 2018; Goto et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2018).

claim: Fruit fly D. melanogaster STING homolog is encoded by the CG1667 gene.
source: Fruit fly D. melanogaster STING homolog is encoded by the CG1667 gene, which we hereafter refer to as dSTING.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the gene encoding Drosophila STING.

claim: dSTING-deficient flies are more susceptible to Listeria infection due to the decreased expression of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs).
source: Particularly, it has been shown that dSTING-deficient flies are more susceptible to Listeria infection due to the decreased expression of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) – small positively charged proteins that possess antimicrobial properties against a variety of microorganisms (Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Martin et al., 2018).

claim: No effect has been observed during Escherichia coli or Micrococcus luteus infections in dSTING-deficient flies.
source: However, no effect has been observed during Escherichia coli or Micrococcus luteus infections (Goto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Goto et al., 2018).

claim: dSTING has been shown to attenuate Zika virus infection in fly brains.
source: dSTING has been shown to attenuate Zika virus infection in fly brains (Liu et al., 2018) and participate in the control of infection by two picorna-like viruses (DCV and CrPV) but not two other RNA viruses FHV and SINV or dsDNA virus IIV6 (Goto et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Liu et al., 2018).

claim: dSTING participates in the control of infection by two picorna-like viruses (DCV and CrPV) but not two other RNA viruses FHV and SINV or dsDNA virus IIV6.
source: dSTING has been shown to attenuate Zika virus infection in fly brains (Liu et al., 2018) and participate in the control of infection by two picorna-like viruses (DCV and CrPV) but not two other RNA viruses FHV and SINV or dsDNA virus IIV6 (Goto et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Goto et al., 2018; Martin et al., 2018).

claim: All these effects are linked to the activation of NF-κB transcription factor Relish.
source: All these effects are linked to the activation of NF-κB transcription factor Relish (Kleino and Silverman, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Kleino and Silverman, 2014).

claim: Immune system is tightly linked with metabolic regulation in all animals.
source: Immune system is tightly linked with metabolic regulation in all animals, and proper re-distribution of the energy is crucial during immune challenges (Odegaard and Chawla, 2013; Alwarawrah et al., 2018; Lee and Lee, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Odegaard and Chawla, 2013; Alwarawrah et al., 2018; Lee and Lee, 2018).

claim: In both flies and humans, excessive immune response can lead to a dysregulation of metabolic stores.
source: In both flies and humans, excessive immune response can lead to a dysregulation of metabolic stores.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between immune response and metabolism.

claim: The loss of metabolic homeostasis can result in weakening of the immune system.
source: Conversely, the loss of metabolic homeostasis can result in weakening of the immune system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between metabolism and immune system.

claim: The mechanistic links between immune system and metabolic regulation are integrated in Drosophila fat body.
source: The mechanistic links between these two important systems are integrated in Drosophila fat body (Arrese and Soulages, 2010; Buchon et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Arrese and Soulages, 2010; Buchon et al., 2014).

claim: Insect fat body stores excess nutrients and mobilizes them during metabolic shifts.
source: Similarly to mammalian liver and adipose tissue, insect fat body stores excess nutrients and mobilizes them during metabolic shifts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect fat body function.

claim: The fat body serves as a major immune organ by producing AMPs during infection.
source: The fat body also serves as a major immune organ by producing AMPs during infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect fat body function.

claim: The fat body is able to switch its transcriptional status from 'anabolic' to 'immune' program.
source: There is an evidence that the fat body is able to switch its transcriptional status from 'anabolic' to 'immune' program (Clark et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Clark et al., 2013).

claim: Triacylglycerols (TAGs) constitute approximately 90% of the stored lipids in fat body.
source: The main fat body components are lipids, with triacylglycerols (TAGs) constituting approximately 90% of the stored lipids (Canavoso et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation (Canavoso et al., 2001).

claim: Most of the TAGs stored in fat body comes from the dietary fat originating from the gut during feeding.
source: Even though most of the TAGs stored in fat body comes from the dietary fat originating from the gut during feeding, de novo lipid synthesis in the fat body also significantly contributes to the pool of storage lipids (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Wicker-Thomas et al., 2015; Parvy et al., 2012; Garrido et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Wicker-Thomas et al., 2015; Parvy et al., 2012; Garrido et al., 2015).

claim: De novo lipid synthesis in the fat body significantly contributes to the pool of storage lipids.
source: Even though most of the TAGs stored in fat body comes from the dietary fat originating from the gut during feeding, de novo lipid synthesis in the fat body also significantly contributes to the pool of storage lipids (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Wicker-Thomas et al., 2015; Parvy et al., 2012; Garrido et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Heier and Kühnlein, 2018; Wicker-Thomas et al., 2015; Parvy et al., 2012; Garrido et al., 2015).

claim: Most of the enzymes involved in metabolism, including lipid metabolism, are evolutionarily and functionally conserved between Drosophila and mammals.
source: Despite the difference in physiology, most of the enzymes involved in metabolism, including lipid metabolism, are evolutionarily and functionally conserved between Drosophila and mammals (Lehmann, 2018; Toprak et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Lehmann, 2018; Toprak et al., 2020).

claim: Major signaling pathways involved in metabolic control, such as insulin system, TOR, steroid hormones, FOXO, and many others, are present in fruit flies.
source: Major signaling pathways involved in metabolic control, such as insulin system, TOR, steroid hormones, FOXO, and many others, are present in fruit flies (Brogiolo et al., 2001; Oldham et al., 2000; Jünger et al., 2003; King-Jones and Thummel, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Brogiolo et al., 2001; Oldham et al., 2000; Jünger et al., 2003; King-Jones and Thummel, 2005).

claim: Drosophila has become a popular model system for studying metabolism and metabolic diseases.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that Drosophila has become a popular model system for studying metabolism and metabolic diseases (Teleman, 2009; Owusu-Ansah and Perrimon, 2014; Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018; Baker and Thummel, 2007; Liu and Huang, 2013; Graham and Pick, 2017; Diop and Bodmer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Teleman, 2009; Owusu-Ansah and Perrimon, 2014; Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018; Baker and Thummel, 2007; Liu and Huang, 2013; Graham and Pick, 2017; Diop and Bodmer, 2015).

claim: The highest level of GFP-dSTING expression was observed in the digestive tract in both adults and larvae.
source: The highest level of the expression was observed in the digestive tract in both adults and larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: GFP-dSTING was expressed at the high level in the larval fat body and adult abdominal carcasses which are enriched in fat body cells.
source: GFP-dSTING was also expressed at the high level in the larval fat body and adult abdominal carcasses which are enriched in fat body cells (Zhao and Karpac, 2017; Molaei et al., 2019; Lórincz et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D and citations (Zhao and Karpac, 2017; Molaei et al., 2019; Lórincz et al., 2017).

claim: The larvae carrying dSTINGΔ deletion were more susceptible to both types of stress (starvation and oxidative).
source: The larvae carrying dSTINGΔ deletion were also more susceptible to both types of stress (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: dSTINGΔ mutant flies consumed food at the same rate as control flies.
source: To test this possibility, we used capillary feeder (CAFE) assay (Ja et al., 2007), which showed that it was not the case, and dSTINGΔ mutant flies consumed food at the same rate as control flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CAFE assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 'Smurf' assay did not reveal any loss of gut wall integrity in dSTINGΔ mutants.
source: 'Smurf' assay did not reveal any loss of gut wall integrity in dSTINGΔ mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Smurf assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.
